analysis.one_liner: Lets cities and towns offer their own broadband by overriding state laws that ban it.
analysis.headline: The Community Broadband Act was introduced in January 2015 with six sponsors, referred to the Senate Commerce Committee, and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the 114th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Many states have laws that stop cities and local utilities from building their own broadband networks. This bill would override those laws, letting any state, city, agency, or Indian tribe offer internet service to residents. To answer the concern that governments would stack the deck, it requires public providers to follow the same rules as private companies, publish notice, take public comment, and give private companies 30 days to bid on any project before a city builds it itself. It also bars federal money from bailing out a failed city broadband project.
analysis.who_benefits: Residents — especially in rural areas and smaller towns where private providers offer slow, expensive, or no service — would gain the option of a city-built or city-owned broadband network. Cities, municipal utilities, and tribal governments would gain the legal right to serve their communities. Private broadband builders would also gain, because the bill requires public projects to invite private bids and encourages public-private partnerships before a city builds anything itself.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Residents of areas with poor internet service

how_it_helps.text: Overrides any state or local law that prohibits or substantially inhibits a public provider — a state, city, agency, or Indian tribe — from offering telecommunications or broadband service to anyone.
Requires public providers to apply permitting, rights-of-way, and other rules without favoring themselves over private competitors, and keeps them subject to all federal communications law.
Before building, a city must publish notice, hold an open process on costs and alternatives, and give private companies 30 days to bid to provide the service themselves.
Bars federal funds from reviving a failed municipal broadband project after bankruptcy or termination, except in federally declared disaster areas.

analysis.who_pays: Incumbent cable and telephone companies would face new public-sector competition in markets that state laws currently keep off limits. Taxpayers in a city that builds a network would bear the financial risk of the project, though the bill bars federal bailout money if it fails.

drawbacks.text: Municipal broadband projects can and do fail; taxpayers in the sponsoring city would bear the risk, a concern the bill itself acknowledges by barring federal funds to revive a bankrupt or terminated project.

Cities would gain a competitor backed by public authority, and private providers argue a government-owned network can tilt the field through its control of rights-of-way and permitting; the bill addresses this only through a non-discrimination rule, not a full separation.
The notice-and-bidding requirements add at least a 30-day process and public hearings before any city project can proceed, which delays service in areas that lack it today.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is a narrow, targeted fix: it removes state-level bans on public broadband while building in the safeguards critics usually demand — equal treatment of private competitors, mandatory bidding opportunities, public input, and no federal bailouts for failures. The main risk is borne locally by the city that builds a network, not by federal or state taxpayers. The upside is competition in markets where, by definition, residents have few or no alternatives.

outcome.mechanism: The bill went straight to the Senate Commerce Committee the day it was introduced and sat there, with no hearing, no markup, and no floor vote, until the 114th Congress ended and it expired.

narrative.text: Sen. Cory Booker introduced the Community Broadband Act on January 22, 2015, joined by Sens. Markey and McCaskill.
The same day, it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation.
Five senators cosponsored the bill: four Democrats and one independent.
No further action was ever taken — the bill never left the committee and expired when the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Incumbent cable and telephone companies are better off: the state laws that shield their markets from municipal competition remain on the books, and no senator was ever asked to vote on ending them.

for.name: Sen. Cory Booker
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led it as sole sponsor.

for.name: Sens. Ed Markey and Claire McCaskill
for.role: U.S. Senators from Missouri and Massachusetts
for.what_they_did: Joined Booker as original cosponsors when the bill was introduced.

against.name: Sen. John Thune
against.role: Chair, Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup of the bill, keeping it from reaching the Senate floor.

against.name: Broadband and cable industry
against.role: Incumbent cable and telephone companies and their trade groups
against.what_they_did: Lobbied against municipal broadband generally and supported the state laws restricting it that this bill would override.

sides.party_line_note: All six sponsors — five Democrats and one independent — were from outside the Republican majority, and the Republican-chaired Commerce Committee took no action on the bill; no Republican cosponsored it.

industries.industry: Cable and broadband providers (Comcast, Charter, AT&T, telephone companies)
industries.note: State laws now ban or hobble city-owned broadband in much of the country; this bill would remove those bans and expose incumbent providers to public-sector competition on price and service. Their interest in keeping those laws runs against residents who want another option.
Cities, towns, agencies, and Indian tribes would gain the right to build and offer broadband to their residents, in areas private providers have not served adequately.
The bill requires public providers to open a 30-day bidding window and encourages public-private partnerships, so private firms would compete to build and run the same networks.
